name: Rosa Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a day at the agency look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm twenty-seven and lead design at a five-person studio making posters, logos and campaign pages for local shops. I have a master's in design, and I use AI every day to sketch directions, then I check the type, ownership and accessibility myself. The best bit is showing a shopkeeper a layout that finally fits their window. The hard bit is that senior responsibility comes with low pay here; I rent a room and have ten days of expenses saved.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How secure is the studio, and who else relies on your wage?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live alone and have no children, so the rent is mine to cover. Last spring a client paid late and we lost a Friday's paid work for two weeks. There are few other design desks nearby, although people keep saying the tools mean anyone can open one. That doesn't pay my landlord.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team that a faster mock-up is useful, but a small shop still needs a designer to ask what belongs on the sign. I won't sell the client an AI picture with a made-up logo. The owner should pay for checking as well as clicking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My lead work probably continues, but ten days saved is frightening if another invoice lands late. Daily AI use already helps me draft, so a plateau would not give me a new advantage. The studio could cut a Friday again without any dramatic technology at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I'll keep checking layouts against the client's actual prices and the print proof, and ask the owner for a written minimum paid week. I'll put thirty from each paid month into a separate rent reserve if wages arrive. In the plateau's first year I'll keep that routine and compare the actual paid Fridays with the written week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the next missed Friday, not about a robot. The design work is here, but ten days' rent money disappears very quickly. A pretty draft cannot buy another week of groceries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened on the missed Fridays?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still fixed a shop poster, but the studio paid four days because the client delayed its bill. I asked for the print charge to be paid before we sent the final files. That protected the printer, not my missing Friday wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a second design job nearby?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would look at an actual paid posting, but there are not many and I will not swap a four-day week for an unpaid trial. For now the written week and a small reserve are concrete. I cannot make another agency open by wishing.

I'd ask the owner for a **written paid week** rather than a promise about Fridays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI can make a dozen layouts before lunch, but the people who commission them should not get free checking from us. I'd join the other designers in asking the owner for paid review hours and a published rota. If clients bring their own AI ads, somebody still has to make the sign readable and legally theirs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My speed may make me useful, yet the studio might sell fewer original campaigns and cut my week. I have no cushion for that experiment. I want to learn the new accessibility checker only if I can test it on our paid jobs and see whether it catches faults I missed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll join the three designers' written request for paid review hours and shift dates. If the owner gives paid time to compare the new AI accessibility checker with printed posters, I'll test it, log false passes and learn it if it catches real faults. I'll keep paid client layouts while the hours exist; in the first year of this slower change I'll ask for the actual rota before committing to another job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious and a little impatient. I can learn a tool quickly, but I cannot learn a missing wage into existence. An accessible poster needs a person able to stop the bad print run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the new checker have to catch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Small text that passed on screen but vanishes on the bus-stop print, and a colour contrast that fails in daylight. I would compare its flags with the actual proof and mark any false pass. A paid test gives us evidence, not a guarantee of future shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your group ask for more than a demonstration?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. The three of us would sign for a paid review rota and authority to hold a print run when the checker is wrong. We would ask for written dates if the owner cuts layout hours. I would not call one private software lesson a worker agreement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my friends full thinking AI by 2028 threatens the design invoices, not just our sketching tricks. Hands-on robots come around 2031, which may leave a short period for human print setup. I'd ask our designers' group to demand written closure dates and any paid transition work rather than a speech about creativity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my lead desk could disappear before I rebuild ten days of savings. Being good with today's tools would not make me the owner of tomorrow's AGI. I could try print finishing, but a physical job is not a magic shelter once the robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I'll join the designers' written request for closure dates and paid transition work, keep any paid layout week and compare our rent with a four-day wage. If the design desk ends in the first year after 2028, I'll apply for a posted paid print-finishing shift only if its written weekly hours and after-travel pay cover rent and essentials. I'll ask to see one paid setup shift if offered, and take the print role only after a signed offer and safe machine instruction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I can move fast, but a ten-day reserve is barely a landing strip. A print shop cannot hire me just because I admire its machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no print shop posts a paid opening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd search other posted paid local work against a written rent budget and keep paid studio shifts while they exist. I would compare both options with the actual weekly bill before moving. If the agency week ends, I would need paid hours somewhere, not a portfolio promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for a machine course first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not on ten days saved. I would ask whether a real paid vacancy offers instruction on the machine and a paid setup observation. I would not claim a certificate buys a shift that has not been posted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years lets us build a real paid exit from the studio instead of asking a tiny agency to promise a future it cannot sell. I would bring print workers and designers together to ask for paid proof and correction hours. The design desk still meets thinking AI in 2031; hands-on print work gets until about 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can use the next few paid years to learn the physical side of a print run. A new title in our studio would not guarantee another wage, and five years of low pay can still leave me with ten days saved. I would rather find out whether a print floor suits me while I can still earn at design.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I'll ask the local print shop whether a posted paid production role offers a paid observation shift, and take it if offered to test noise, safe duties and the journey. I'll keep paid agency work and join the designers and printers' shared request for paid human proofing hours. In the first year after 2031, if design hours are cut, I'll apply for a still-posted paid production role only if its written weekly hours and after-travel pay cover rent and essentials; I'll leave only after a signed offer and safe machine instruction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but more methodical than in the two-year version. A print proof with an actual cut line would tell me more than an agency title. It would also tell me if my route is wrong before my design wage goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the paid observation is refused?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep whatever paid agency hours remain and check other posted paid work against my written rent budget. I cannot spend ten days of savings waiting outside a print shop. I could still ask another printer, but an unanswered email is not a shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the group request actually change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would ask clients to budget paid proofing and give a named worker authority to stop a wrong print run. Designers and printers would sign the request together. I do not want a free committee that leaves everyone else's paid hours unchanged.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the designers that ten years is enough to ask who owns the work we make with these tools. I would still want paid human review for public signs, where an unreadable notice has a real cost. Thinking AI arrives by 2036 in this picture, before hands-on robots around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be thirty-seven, not old enough to live on a thin reserve, and I cannot assume my design income lasts the decade. Ten years could let me build a steadier budget and a trade I can actually do. It could also let me put off the hard decision until the client list vanishes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From 2026 I'll save forty from each paid month toward three months of rent, and keep a yearly record of paid design weeks and client losses. I'll work with other designers to ask clients for paid correction hours and use our real print-proof errors as evidence. In the first year after 2036, if AGI ends my design hours, I'll seek posted paid local production or service work against my written rent budget; I won't count a future co-op or my family as a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about another unpaid Friday and how easy it is to drift. A long calendar gives me time to build savings, if the agency pays enough months. Ten years is not a rent account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you start a design co-op?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would talk with two designers about shared proofing work, but I would not spend rent money to register a firm without paid clients. If a paid shared job appears, we can price it. A conversation is not an investment yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if your savings target is missed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the target visible and check actual wages each year, not invent a pension or expect a relative to cover the room. If the agency cuts weeks before 2036, I'd bring the job search forward using posted paid openings and the same rent budget. The longer warning helps only if I respond to the real pay record.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because design pay could go before I have enough rent saved to search. Written closure dates, paid transition work and an actual posted print or other job would help. I cannot eat the promise of a creative future.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who pays for checking an AI sign before it goes into a public street. A small agency can call that work invisible and then invoice nothing for it. The person who finds the mistake needs paid hours and the right to stop the print run.

headlineQuote: The person who finds the mistake needs paid hours and the right to stop the print run.

She pushes for **paid human proofing** and tests new tools against printed errors with colleagues.
Fast AGI threatens her **design wage**; more warning lets her test posted print work and build a rent reserve.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end her design pay before she has enough rent saved to search.
